question: Is there an opportunity to change course in Syria because of that?
options: There is no opening to shift our strategy because Bashar al-Assad remains entirely dependent on Vladimir Putin and Tehran to hold Damascus, and neither of them has any intention of targeting extremists. When Secretary Kerry met with Sergey Lavrov in Geneva, we saw that diplomacy achieved nothing for the Free Syrian Army in Aleppo. The Pentagon and General Joseph Dunford know that partnering with Moscow only alienates Turkey and our Gulf partners in Riyadh, so shifting course now would be a strategic disaster.

We have a major opportunity to shift course because President Bashar al-Assad has defeated the radical Islamist elements in Idlib and Daraa, leaving a unified Syrian Arab Army ready to secure the border. Ambassador Staffan de Mistura at the United Nations told the Security Council that moderate opposition groups in Homs are willing to negotiate a lasting peace in Geneva. If President-elect Trump works with Tehran and Moscow, we can stabilize the region and defeat foreign jihadists permanently.

There is no reason to alter our policy since Bashar al-Assad and Vladimir Putin have already destroyed the moderate opposition in Aleppo and eastern Ghouta with Iranian militias. Vice President Joe Biden and Secretary Ashton Carter both warned the Senate Armed Services Committee that Moscow only wants to prop up the Ba'ath party dictatorship, not fight extremists. If Washington trusts the Kremlin or the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, we abandon our Kurdish allies in the Syrian Democratic Forces and betray every democratic value we hold dear.

President-elect Trump can coordinate airstrikes with Vladimir Putin and the Syrian Arab Army against al-Nusra Front in Idlib, which creates an opening to pivot our approach. General Michael Flynn and other national security advisors understand that fighting both Damascus and ISIS simultaneously in Palmyra and Deir ez-Zor makes no strategic sense. We can finally end the civil war, secure the borders, and stop wasting resources on corrupt rebel factions backed by foreign intelligence agencies by aligning with Russia and the regime.
why: Answer 1 argues that there is an opportunity to change course under the new administration, whereas Answer 2 argues that there is no opening to shift strategy and doing so would be a disaster.

Answer 1 argues that Russia and the Assad regime are not actually fighting ISIS and that their tactics empower extremists, whereas Answer 2 asserts that Assad has successfully defeated radical Islamist elements and that cooperating with him presents an opportunity to stabilize the region.

Answer 1 argues that there is an opportunity to change course based on Donald Trump's campaign statements, whereas Answer 2 argues there is no reason to alter current policy because doing so would betray democratic values and allies.

Answer 1 argues that aligning with Russia and the Assad regime is a flawed approach because they do not actually fight ISIS, whereas Answer 2 advocates for US coordination with Russia and the regime precisely because fighting both Damascus and ISIS makes no strategic sense.
